name: Felt-Remnant
geological_features: Ancient impact basin covering 40% of surface
specific_features: Surface material with compressed, matted texture resembling industrial felt
Fragment of a larger body destroyed in ancient collision
description: Felt-Remnant is a small, irregular body that is clearly a fragment of a much larger world destroyed in a cataclysmic collision billions of years ago. Its surface material has been compressed and matted by the impact forces into a dense, fibrous texture that resembles industrial felt, with mineral fibers interlocked at the microscopic level in ways that should not occur naturally. The body is roughly spherical but with a distinctly flattened face on one side, the fracture surface where it separated from its parent world, now weathered by eons of micrometeorite bombardment but still recognizably artificial in its geometry.

Without atmosphere or significant gravity, Felt-Remnant offers no comfort to visitors. The surface is dark, nearly black, absorbing what little light reaches this distant orbit. Temperatures never rise above minus forty Celsius even in direct sunlight. The fractured face reveals the body's internal structure in cross-section: layers of compressed material surrounding a core of exposed crystalline minerals that glitter when illuminated, the frozen heart of a dead world laid bare to the void.

Spectroscopic analysis of Felt-Remnant's parent body, reconstructed from this fragment and others found in similar orbits, suggests it was once a medium-sized rocky planet with a differentiated core and active geology. The collision that destroyed it was likely with another planetary body of similar size, an event of almost incomprehensible violence that reduced both worlds to rubble. Felt-Remnant is the largest surviving fragment, and its compressed surface material preserves a record of the impact forces involved—pressures and temperatures that briefly exceeded those found in stellar cores.

The platinum group metals exposed in the fracture face are of exceptional purity, concentrated by the same forces that compressed the surface material. Small-scale mining operations have been extracting these metals for years, carefully cutting into the matted surface with plasma tools. Miners report that the material resists cutting in unusual ways, the interlocked fibers distributing force and blunting conventional tools rapidly. The body is a tombstone for a lost world, slowly being dismantled for its bones, and no one has yet found any trace of whether the destroyed planet ever harbored life.
